details:
**Crucifixion under Pontius Pilate**
Jesus was executed by crucifixion in Jerusalem on the orders of Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea, who washed his hands to show he was not responsible. During the execution Roman soldiers cast lots for his clothes, he wore a crown of thorns, the repentant thief (traditionally named Dismas) asked to be remembered, and the Temple veil was torn from top to bottom when he died.

**Isa ibn Maryam**
The name for Jesus in Islam, meaning "Jesus son of Mary." Muslims honor him as the second-to-last prophet before Muhammad and as the Messiah, but Sura 5 (Al-Ma'ida) stresses he was "no more than a messenger," not the son of God. Sura 4 (An-Nisa) says he was not truly crucified; instead God raised him into heaven.

**Qur'anic miracles: speaking from the cradle and clay birds**
In the Qur'an, the infant Jesus speaks from his cradle to defend his mother Mary's honor, and he shapes birds from clay and breathes life into them. Sura 19 (Maryam) tells of his virgin birth, during which Mary is told to shake a palm tree for dates, and in Sura 5 he asks God to send down a table of food from heaven.

**Return with the Mahdi and slaying of the Dajjal**
Islamic eschatology holds that Jesus will return near the end of time, pray behind the Mahdi, and kill the Dajjal (the false messiah). An empty grave space beside Muhammad's tomb under the Green Dome in Medina is traditionally said to be reserved for him; the Ahmadiyya instead believe he survived the cross and is buried at the Roza Bal shrine in Kashmir.

**Resurrection and the empty tomb**
Christians believe Jesus rose from the dead on the third day after the crucifixion. He had been laid in a tomb belonging to Joseph of Arimathea, and the stone was found rolled away; Matthew says the chief priests bribed the guards to claim the body was stolen, and Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 15 that faith is futile without the resurrection.

**Sign of Jonah**
When asked for a sign, Jesus said that the only sign given would be the "sign of Jonah": just as Jonah spent three days in the belly of the great fish, the Son of Man would spend three days in the heart of the earth, a prediction of his death and resurrection.

**Saul on the road to Damascus (Book of Acts)**
In Acts, the risen Jesus appears to Saul of Tarsus, asking "Why are you persecuting me?" and blinding him, then sends Ananias to restore his sight; Saul becomes the apostle Paul. Acts also opens with Jesus promising the Holy Spirit and ascending into heaven, and Paul later quotes him saying "It is more blessed to give than to receive" and "it is hard for you to kick against the goads."

**Stations of the Cross and the Seven Last Words**
On his way to Calvary, Jesus met his mother, fell three times, was helped carrying the cross by Simon of Cyrene, and had his face wiped by Veronica; these scenes are among the Stations of the Cross. Seven sayings he spoke on the cross are known as the Seven Last Words, with labels such as the "Word of Relationship" and the "Word of Triumph" ("It is finished").

**Shroud of Turin and the True Cross**
The Shroud of Turin is a linen cloth believed by some to be Jesus's burial shroud, bearing an image and bloodstains; Secondo Pia's 1898 photograph revealed a striking negative image. The True Cross is the relic of the cross itself, which St. Helena, mother of Constantine, was said to have found in Jerusalem after destroying a temple to Venus on the site.

**Nativity in Bethlehem**
Jesus was born in Bethlehem to the Virgin Mary and laid in a manger. Shepherds came to adore him, the Magi brought gold, frankincense, and myrrh, and Herod's Massacre of the Innocents followed; Isaiah's prophecies of a child called Immanuel who "shall eat curds and honey" and named "Wonderful Counselor" are read as foretelling his birth.

**Baptism in the Jordan River**
Jesus was baptized by John the Baptist in the Jordan River. As he came out of the water, the Holy Spirit descended on him in the form of a dove and a voice from heaven declared him God's beloved Son.

**Parables**
Jesus taught through short stories called parables, including the Good Samaritan (a Samaritan helps a wounded man that a priest and a Levite ignored on the road to Jericho), the Prodigal Son, the Rich Man and Lazarus, and the Ten Virgins, five of whom run out of lamp oil and are locked out of a wedding feast.

**Josephus and Suetonius**
Non-Christian ancient sources used as evidence that Jesus existed. In Book 20 of Antiquities of the Jews, Josephus mentions James as "the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ," while the Roman historian Suetonius mentions a "Chrestus," a spelling that makes it unclear whether he meant Christ.

**Quest for the historical Jesus**
The scholarly effort to reconstruct Jesus's life as a historical person, shaped by Albert Schweitzer's 1906 book The Quest of the Historical Jesus. Scholars use tests such as the "criterion of embarrassment," and the Jesus Seminar, whose members included film director Paul Verhoeven, voted on which sayings were authentic.

**Temptation in the desert and finding in the Temple**
After his baptism, Jesus fasted for 40 days in the desert and resisted Satan's temptations, replying "Man does not live by bread alone." As a boy, he went missing during a trip to Jerusalem and was found sitting among the teachers in the Temple.
